---
title: "Protein structure"
description: "Inspect protein structures and connect quantitative candidates to structural context."
---

## Purpose

Use **Toolkits → Protein structure** for general structural interpretation after a candidate protein has been identified. This page focuses on how to connect a protein, mutation, PTM, domain, or other candidate feature to structural context.

For **Swiss-Model sequence submission and model prediction**, use **Toolkits → SwissModel**. The Swiss-Model interface screenshot and step-by-step modeling instructions are maintained on that dedicated page.

## Recommended workflow

1. Resolve the candidate to a stable protein identifier and confirm the expected protein sequence.
2. Obtain an experimental structure or an appropriate predicted model.
3. Confirm chain and residue numbering before mapping mutations, PTMs, domains, or functional residues.
4. Inspect the three-dimensional context and any relevant quality/confidence information.
5. Record the structure source, model/entry identifier, and quality evidence in the figure legend or Methods.

## Interpretation

Structural visualization is most useful when it is tied back to the biological question. For example, a differentially abundant protein may be examined for whether a candidate mutation or PTM lies near an active site, interface, conserved domain, or structurally constrained region.

::: {.callout-tip}
For a ProtVis-generated Swiss-Model prediction, continue to **Toolkits → SwissModel** for sequence submission, project information, model-quality results, PDB information, Ramachandran diagnostics, residue composition, 3D visualization, and downloads.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
Predicted structures and experimentally determined structures are not equivalent evidence. When using a model, report its source and relevant confidence/quality metrics and avoid over-interpreting poorly supported regions.
:::
